summary.text: Achilles held funeral games for Patroclus and dragged Hector's body daily — until old Priam came alone through the camp at night, kissed the hands that had killed his son, and ransomed the body; Troy buried Hector, and the Iliad ends with the hero's rites.

chapters.title: Games for Patroclus
chapters.text: Book 23 opens with the pyre: Achilles sacrificed horses, dogs, and twelve Trojan captives on Patroclus' funeral mound. After the bones were gathered in a golden urn, the Achaeans held games — chariot race won by Diomedes after Athena broke Eumelus' car, boxing, wrestling, foot-race, armed combat, archery, and throwing the spear. Antilochus of Nestor's house outwitted Menelaus in the chariot turn; Ajax and Odysseus drew in the wrestling. The games honoured the companion whose death had ended Achilles' wrath against Agamemnon and begun the wrath against Hector.

chapters.title: The body dragged
chapters.text: Each day Achilles dragged Hector's corpse behind his chariot around Patroclus' tomb — and each night Apollo preserved the body from corruption, for Hera and the Achaeans would have had the dogs devour it. The gods on Olympus pitied the outrage; Zeus sent Thetis to tell Achilles to accept ransom, and Iris to bid Priam go. The nested episode on Achilles and Hector tells the killing; here the poem turns from vengeance to pity.

chapters.title: Priam in the camp
chapters.text: Priam loaded a wagon with treasure and crossed the plain with Idaios the herald, guided by Hermes in the likeness of a young man. They passed the sentries and reached Achilles' hut; the old king kissed the hands that had killed his children — the hands that had slain Hector — and asked for the body. Achilles wept with him, remembering his own father Peleus and the son he would never see grow old. He raised the body on a bier, covered it, and bound the kings not to delay the truce.

chapters.title: Hector's rites
chapters.text: Priam drove through the camp while Achilles kept the host from pursuit. In Troy, Andromache and Hecuba and Helen lamented over the body on the bier — the wife who had begged him not to fight, the queen, the cause of the war who honoured him most truly. For nine days they gathered wood; on the tenth they burned Hector and buried the bones, then feasted in the palace. The Iliad ends with the rites of Troy's shield — the war would go on, but Homer's poem closes on burial and grief, not on the horse or the fall of the city.
